situation.roe_position: Return on equity is high now (24.8% in 2025, about 16.6% annualized in 2026) mainly because of strong Two Sigma Hamilton Fund returns on top of a combined ratio in the low-to-mid 90s. Underwriting income is thin relative to investment income (9-month underwriting income $102.2m against net investment income $323.3m), and the market is softening in property and some specialty lines. Return on equity should drift down toward a mid-teens or lower level as investment results normalise and pricing eases. It should still stay above the 9.36% cost of equity.
situation.why: The 2025 return of 24.8% is the top of the 2022-2025 range and was lifted by fund gains, so it is not a steady level. Hamilton paid a $2.00 special dividend and bought back stock while growing gross premiums written about 15%, so capital does not appear to limit growth in book equity. Book equity growth is therefore set mainly by earnings less payouts, and it is slowed by non-controlling-interest leakage and a soft Q3 underwriting result.

risks.risk: The Two Sigma Hamilton Fund underperforms or has a drawdown, or the company cannot withdraw capital from it. Investment profit drove most of 2025 and 2026 earnings.
Reserve strengthening in long-tail casualty (social inflation) or a major catastrophe, in a softening market, permanently lowers underwriting margins.
Faster premium growth, or a reserve or rating shock, absorbs capital, or the company keeps paying large special dividends and buybacks, so book growth differs from my path.

situation.roe_position: Return on equity is high because of strong investment gains, not underwriting alone. The Two Sigma Hamilton Fund (TSHF) returned $353.2 million year to date, against $102.2 million of underwriting income. Underwriting margins are thinning (Q3 combined ratio 97.3%, underwriting income $15.5 million) as property and specialty pricing softens. Part of the fund's profit goes to non-controlling interest, which lowers income to common. 2025 (24.8%) was the high point. I expect 2026 near 16% and a fade toward the low-to-mid teens.
situation.why: Hamilton paid a $2.00 special dividend (about $200 million in cash), bought back stock and still grew common equity, so regulatory capital is not binding on payouts. Gross premiums written grew 14.9% and the company is adding to its retained book, but Bermuda Monetary Authority (BMA) solvency ratios are not in the packet. Book growth is therefore set by earnings less discretionary dividends and buybacks. The special dividend probably will not repeat at the same size.
